headline_marked: Chrome on Android [[finally gets a back button]] in Version 150
headline: Chrome on Android finally gets a back button in Version 150
summary: After years of user requests, Google Chrome for Android has added a dedicated back button to its interface, bringing it closer to desktop functionality.
details: Google Chrome version 150 for Android is rolling out now, bringing a long-requested feature: a dedicated back button. This update aims to improve navigation for users who prefer a traditional back button over swipe gestures.

The new back button is located within the three-dot menu, positioned to the left of the forward, favorite, download, and reload buttons. This change also means the 'info' button has been moved to the 'Site controls' overflow menu.

The 'Add to home screen' feature has been renamed to 'Install and create shortcut', though its functionality remains the same. This update brings the Android version of Chrome closer in user experience to its desktop counterpart.

While Chrome on iOS has featured a back button for some time, its addition to the Android version is a significant usability improvement for many users. The update is available for those with automatic updates enabled or can be manually downloaded from the Play Store.

headline_marked: [[OpenAI accused of lying]] to court about ChatGPT copyright infringement evidence
headline: OpenAI accused of lying to court about ChatGPT copyright infringement evidence
summary: News organizations allege OpenAI concealed its ability to search ChatGPT logs for copyrighted content, potentially impacting the fair use defense in a high-profile copyright trial.
details: OpenAI is facing calls for "serious sanctions" after allegedly misleading news organizations and the court for years regarding its ability to search ChatGPT logs for evidence of copyright infringement. News outlets, led by The New York Times, claim the AI firm concealed that it had already conducted searches of large log samples prior to litigation.

The allegations surfaced during a re-deposition of an OpenAI privacy engineer, who reportedly revealed that the company had two large, de-identified log samples (10 million and 78 million logs) that could have been shared early in the discovery process. News plaintiffs argue this concealment prolonged discovery and inflated expenses.

According to The New York Times, OpenAI allegedly pretended it lacked the technical ability to search these logs, forcing plaintiffs to spend months in a restricted 'sandbox' with a smaller, heavily redacted sample of 20 million logs. This sample was further skewed by OpenAI's extensive redactions, rendering it "unusable" according to the court.

News plaintiffs' lead counsel stated that OpenAI's actions were an attempt to obstruct access to logs and distort evidence to shield its fair use claims. They argue that if OpenAI truly believed its copying of journalism was legal, it would not have hidden the fact that it had already performed such searches.

An OpenAI spokesperson countered that the sanctions motion is a litigation tactic by the NYT to access more logs and invade user privacy. They suggested the NYT's case is weakening, evidenced by dropped claims, and that OpenAI will continue to defend user privacy and fair use principles.
